title: Beta-agonist Use and Increased Asthma Mortality: Reality or Fiction?
authors: Zhao N, Suissa S, Ernst P
authorConflicts: S. Suissa attended scientific advisory committee meetings or received speaking fees from AstraZeneca, Atara, Boehringer-Ingelheim, Bristol-Myers-Squibb, Merck, Novartis, Panalgo, Pfizer and Seqirus; the other two authors declare no conflicts.
result: Editorial. Recalls a Saskatchewan cohort in which asthma death rose with inhaled short-acting beta-agonist use, sharply above 1.7 canisters per month, and a later population cohort in which regular inhaled corticosteroid use substantially reduced asthma deaths, suggesting that under-use of inhaled corticosteroid was the more likely cause of the association between death and overuse. Of the SABINA Swedish cohort (hazard ratios 2.3 for all-cause and 31.7, 95% CI 11.9 to 84.7, for asthma-related mortality with 11 or more canisters), states that the association must be interpreted with caution because it is also consistent with confounding by disease severity and the analysis did not account for concurrent inhaled corticosteroid use. Notes that a non-eosinophilic subgroup responds to bronchodilators but not corticosteroids, in small studies, and concludes that the role of beta-agonist bronchodilators may need re-examination as asthma heterogeneity is characterised.
